title: Axion Labs — inference capacity & isolation playbook sync
summary: Discovery focused on Axion's reserved GPU needs for production LLM features. Covered traffic profile, isolation requirements for regulated models, warm-pool/prewarm strategies for burst traffic, fallback to hosted variants, and security/compliance pathways (VPC, KMS, SOC2). Agreed to run a 2-week pilot with a reserved small node pool and distributed load profile; Redwood to share pricing, dedicated topology diagram, and security questionnaire.
action_items: Jordan Blake — send dedicated pricing worksheet and topology diagram (due: 2025-08-22)
Priya Nair — share draft pilot runbook and metric collection template (due: 2025-08-21)
Lena Ortiz — provide hourly traffic histogram + 7-day spike events from prod (due: 2025-08-20)
Alex Rivera — confirm KMS provider details and any IP allowlist constraints (due: 2025-08-22)
next_steps: Redwood to propose 2-week pilot plan (reserved 2xA100-equivalent nodes, warm pool, canary routing).
Customer to share traffic histograms and security questionnaire answers.
Schedule pilot kickoff next Tue (tentative) — SE-led baseline tests and latency profiling.
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Blake (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros — I'm Jordan from Redwood. Priya's our solutions engineer, Marcus is on the call too.
[00:10] Dr. Noah Patel (CTO): Hey all, Noah here. We're trying to understand options between hosted, dedicated and private for our inference backbone. Latency matters but cost is a big constraint.
[00:22] Lena Ortiz (Eng Manager): Right, our product team wants sub-200ms median for chat completions, tail less than 500, but we still need to keep cost within the current infra budget.
[00:32] Priya Nair (SE): Makes sense. Can you run through current stack and traffic shape? That helps with sizing reserved pools vs burst strategy.
[00:40] Lena Ortiz: Sure — we run on AWS, EKS + K8s autoscaling for our app tier. For LLM we currently call a mix of the public hosted APIs and one on-prem rig that we spin up for big batches. Production steady-state is ~30 qps, but we have spikes up to ~220 qps during triggers — e.g., nightly batch jobs and product launches. Spikes last 3-7 minutes usually, sometimes 20.
[01:05] Alex Rivera (SRE): Those spikes are the pain point; cold-starts and queueing kill latency. We want prewarm or warm pool so model is hot.
[01:12] Jordan Blake: Ok — so reserved capacity could solve steady state and warm pool handles spikes. How sensitive are you to eviction or noisy neighbor effects? Do you need strict tenant isolation?
[01:22] Dr. Noah Patel: For our healthcare clients we need tenant isolation per client for certain models running PHI. For others, shared tenancy is OK as long as we have logical isolation and audit logs.
[01:32] Priya Nair: Got it. Redwood Dedicated supports strict node-level isolation or soft tenant fencing. For PHI you can opt for dedicated nodes per tenant or dedicated model variants in a VPC/private deployment. We can integrate with your KMS for key isolation and provide audit logs.
[01:48] Lena Ortiz: How fast can we scale warm pool? Our spike profile includes sudden bursts triggered by events, not just scheduled jobs.
[01:55] Priya Nair: We typically recommend a small prewarmed hot pool sized to handle X% of your normal spike and then autoscale from there for larger surges. Prewarm helps avoid KV cache cold starts and kernel JIT overhead. For the kind of 3-7 minute spikes you described, a hot pool with ~2–4 nodes usually eliminates cold penalties for the first wave.
[02:15] Alex Rivera: What about fallback? If dedicated is saturated, can requests route to hosted Redwood model variants automatically?
[02:22] Marcus Chen (Solutions Eng): Yes — smart routing policy can failover to a compatible hosted variant. You can set routing by latency SLO or cost threshold. Failover preserves availability but may change model variant or precision — we emit headers so the app can detect fallback.
[02:38] Dr. Noah Patel: That helps. One concern: encryption and key management. We use AWS KMS CMKs in a shared account. Does Redwood Dedicated support customer KMS?
[02:47] Priya Nair: Yes, KMS integrations are standard for Private and Dedicated; we can either integrate your KMS or run with our managed keys depending on contract. For PHI we recommend customer-managed keys and HSM-backed operations.
[02:58] Lena Ortiz: On compliance: do you have SOC2? What about audit logs retention?
[03:04] Jordan Blake: Redwood is SOC2 Type II and we provide configurable audit log retention. For Dedicated/Private we can align retention windows and forward logs to your SIEM via S3 or a streaming connector. We'll share the security questionnaire.
[03:16] Alex Rivera: Great. Back to sizing — can you run an example sizing sketch? Say 30 qps steady, 220 qps peaks, model is a 13B that runs roughly 40 tokens/s per GPU (approx), average 80 tokens per request.
[03:32] Priya Nair: Quick napkin math: 80 tokens / 40 tokens/s = 2s per request per GPU. 30 qps means about 60s of GPU compute per second — need multiple GPUs. For concurrency, with batching you can handle higher qps per GPU but latency tradeoffs apply. For bursts to 220 qps, a warm pool sized to handle the first 140 qps removes the initial cold penalty; autoscale covers the rest. Depending on batching settings, we'd estimate reserved capacity of 3–4 A100-equivalent GPUs + a warm pool of 2 nodes.
[04:02] Lena Ortiz: Can you explain warm pool eviction and cost implications?
[04:06] Priya Nair: Warm pool means nodes stay running but with idle resources; you pay for them. We offer burst credits and short-duration prewarm options to reduce cost — e.g., keep a tiny hot pool for immediate spikes and spin up burst nodes that are billed at burst rates. There's also a preemptible path but that risks interruptions.
[04:23] Dr. Noah Patel: Our finance team will push back on paying for idle GPUs. Are there metered approaches that still meet latency SLOs?
[04:31] Marcus Chen: Hybrid approach: reserved baseline capacity for steady-state, smaller hot pool for first waves, and aggressive autoscale with fast spin-up in your region. Also caching at prefix level reduces token compute by satisfying repeated prompts. Redwood Optimize can recommend batching and quantization to cut CPU/GPU cost.
[04:50] Alex Rivera: Any network constraints? We're inside a locked VPC with strict egress policies.
[04:55] Priya Nair: Dedicated supports VPC peering and Private deployment with a customer-managed control plane. We can provide NAT or private endpoints and support IP allowlists. We'll map those requirements in the security doc.
[05:06] Lena Ortiz: Timeline: we want to pilot within 2–3 weeks, prove latency and cost, then commit to 6 months reserved if numbers look good.
[05:14] Jordan Blake: That timeline is reasonable. Proposed pilot: 2-week run, reserved 2 GPUs (A100-equivalent) for baseline, 2-node warm pool, data plane in your VPC, collection of latency and cost metrics. Priya will own the runbook.
[05:30] Dr. Noah Patel: What about model versions and rollback? We often iterate models weekly.
[05:35] Priya Nair: Redwood Dedicated supports model pinning and rollouts — canary and A/B. You can pin a model version to the reserved nodes and have automated rollback to hosted if the new version regresses. We'll also capture quality metrics tied to your prompt set.
[05:50] Alex Rivera: During pilot, we want to run a synthetic traffic replay to validate tail latencies. Can Redwood run that from our data?
[05:57] Marcus Chen: Absolutely — we can ingest request traces or a synthetic generator; Priya will coordinate the profiling and tracing hooks.
[06:05] Lena Ortiz: Pricing: high level, what's the delta between reserved vs on-demand and warm pool costs?
[06:11] Jordan Blake: We'll share the pricing worksheet. High-level: reserved monthly commit gives you the best per-GPU rate, warm pool is charged as reserved compute plus a smaller management fee; burst nodes are billed at a premium. We'll send examples based on your expected hours.
[06:26] Alex Rivera: Are there any performance regressions with quantized models? We need to know quality tradeoffs.
[06:32] Priya Nair: Quantization often gives 2–3x throughput improvements with small quality delta depending on model. Redwood Optimize will recommend quantization profiles per workload and we can run evals against your prompt set during the pilot to measure regressions.
[06:46] Dr. Noah Patel: From a procurement perspective, contract length? We might want 6 or 12 months reserved if pilot goes well. Any early termination penalties?
[06:54] Jordan Blake: Standard reserved contracts have minimum commit period; specifics to be included in proposal. For pilots we can do a short-term eval without heavy legal.
[07:03] Lena Ortiz: Ok, let's surface risks — what happens if the warm pool fails to scale on a massive traffic surge?
[07:09] Priya Nair: Two layers of protection: routing fallback to hosted models and automatic capacity rebalancing; plus we can set rate limits per tenant to preserve latency for priority traffic. We'll work with you on SLAs and fallback behavior.
[07:24] Alex Rivera: Also need a runbook for incident response and on-call contacts.
[07:28] Jordan Blake: We'll include a contacts sheet and escalation path in the pilot runbook.
[07:33] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[07:36] Priya Nair: Quick note on prewarming: for some model families, we persist KV cache snapshots to accelerate warm-up across restarts — we call it prefix caching. That can shave 100-300ms on first tokens depending on prompt patterns.
[07:52] Lena Ortiz: Nice. Any gotchas with our EKS setup?
[07:55] Marcus Chen: Only if you try to tightly integrate autoscaling at the app layer; better to route through Redwood for inference and keep the model layer managed. We'll provide a minimal sidecar SDK to collect traces and metrics.
[08:07] Alex Rivera: For audit logs, we want 12 months retention and ability to export to our Splunk.
[08:12] Jordan Blake: That's doable; we'll note it in the security attachment.
[08:17] Dr. Noah Patel: Ok let's recap next steps.
[08:20] Jordan Blake: Recap: Redwood to send pricing worksheet, dedicated topology diagram, security questionnaire, and pilot runbook. Axion to share traffic histogram, KMS details, and grant access to synthetic traces. Pilot kickoff targeted next Tue.
[08:33] Lena Ortiz: Sounds good. Thanks all.
[08:35] Jordan Blake: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up by EOD with the docs.
[47:30] [call ends]
